section_summary: This section begins with Domei wartime bulletins from December 1943 reporting Japanese military claims in the Pacific and China, administration in occupied Asian territories, Japanese–Thai relations, and Japan’s protest over the sinking of the hospital ship Buenos Aires Maru. Most of the section consists of reports by U.S. Embassy Second Secretary Gerald Warner translating and commenting on Japanese-language newspapers in Argentina, with extensive coverage of espionage investigations, the rupture of Argentine–Japanese relations, repatriation, community associations, elections, finances, businesses, schools, and propaganda. A Department of State letter and memorandum discuss the routing and significance of these press summaries, and the final page begins another translation report covering June 1944.

subfiles.title: Domei war and Shonan administration bulletin, continuation
subfiles.about: Continuation of a bulletin on Shonan’s consultative board and Japanese claims concerning Army and Navy results since December 1941.
subfiles.summary: Continuation: Shonan's mayor inducts a fifteen-member consultative board as evidence of popular participation, then propagandistic totals of claimed Japanese victories and Allied losses, with hundreds of warships and thousands of aircraft allegedly destroyed.

subfiles.title: The Domei News, Ankara, December 20, 1943
subfiles.about: Bulletin on teacher training in Johor, Malay defense mobilization, fighting in Shanxi, and the Japanese account of the Battle of Tarawa and Makin.
subfiles.summary: Domei News, Ankara, December 20, 1943: retraining Johor teachers in Japanese methods, Malay editor Ishak urging youth to join defense units, Nationalist claims against Communists in the Taihang Mountains, and a Japanese account of the Tarawa and Makin battles ending in Shibazaki's last charge.

subfiles.title: The Domei News, Ankara, December 21, 1943
subfiles.about: Reports on Indian military training, the Philippine budget, public health works in Jakarta, and Japanese economic policy in occupied Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Indian residents in Kluang are said to be establishing military-training centers, while the Philippine National Assembly passes its 1944 budget and tax legislation. The bulletin describes municipal sanitation work in Jakarta. Governor-General Rensuke Isogai reviews Hong Kong’s industries and finances and calls for increased wartime trade to support Japan.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d’informations, Agence Domei, December 21, 1943
subfiles.about: French-language bulletin commemorating the second anniversary of the Japanese–Thai alliance and reporting the Japanese ambassador’s return to Burma.
subfiles.summary: Domei, December 21, 1943: Japanese and Thai officials celebrate the alliance with a Tokyo luncheon, ceremonies in Bangkok and messages, Shigemitsu calling it a step toward Greater East Asia; Ambassador Sawada returns to Rangoon after Tokyo consultations on Burma policy.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d’information on the Buenos Aires Maru protest
subfiles.about: Japanese diplomatic protest over the sinking of the hospital ship Buenos Aires Maru, followed by a short report on agricultural planning near Jakarta.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Foreign Ministry communique alleges a U.S. B-24 bombed the marked hospital ship Buenos Aires Maru on November 27, 1943 and survivors were strafed, violating the Hague and Geneva conventions, demanding punishment and assurances; recalls an Arabia Maru protest; pages 134-135 duplicate; a final item on agricultural experts.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d’informations, Agence Domei, December 23, 1943
subfiles.about: Bulletin combining Japanese combat claims in New Britain and New Guinea with administrative and economic reports from the Philippines and the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Domei, December 23, 1943: claimed Allied ships and aircraft destroyed near Cape Merkus, Alexishafen, Wewak, Madang and Finschhafen; a new Philippine information bureau, South Sulawesi tobacco, Jakarta sanitation, and Claro Recto's proposal for diplomacy and administration training.

subfiles.title: Imperial Headquarters communiqués, December 22–23, 1943
subfiles.about: Imperial Headquarters claims concerning raids on Kunming and Yunnan and attacks on an Allied convoy near Cape Merkus.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Headquarters communiques, December 22-23, 1943: seventeen aircraft claimed destroyed at Kunming and Yunnan airfields, and ships, craft and aircraft claimed hit near Cape Merkus, with ten Japanese aircraft failing to return.

subfiles.title: Bulletin d’information, Agence Domei, December 24, 1943
subfiles.about: Reports on Christmas in Manila, a downed aircraft near Mengzi, and the conclusion of a Philippine medical congress.
subfiles.summary: Domei, December 24, 1943: public Christmas events hosted by President and Mrs. Laurel, an Allied aircraft shot down near Heimingwo, and Antonio Sison closing a medical congress praising cancer and tuberculosis research and local chemical manufacture.

subfiles.title: The Domei News, Ankara, December 23, 1943
subfiles.about: English-language bulletin on Axis commemorations, air raids on Bangkok, fighting in China and New Britain, and construction of the Kanmon tunnel.
subfiles.summary: Domei News, Ankara, December 23, 1943: Italian Fascists visit Yasukuni, a Thai spokesman condemns bombing of Bangkok, claimed Japanese air superiority at Changde and revised Cape Merkus results, and Kanmon railway tunnel workers nearly breaking through.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, September 16–18, 1943
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Translations and skeptical commentary on Japanese-language press reports concerning Italy’s surrender, Axis diplomacy, military claims, antisemitism, and Japanese opinion in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The report follows Japanese reactions to the Badoglio government, seizure of Italian vessels, and the positioning of Italian diplomatic missions, alongside celebrations of Manchukuo and numerous combat claims from the Pacific, China, and Burma. It notes an antisemitic series by Taniguchi, editorials flattering Argentine neutrality, and commentary on Japanese Americans in the United States. Other items include the sinking of Yamato Maru, the Tottori earthquake, delayed mail via Siberia, and an arsenal explosion near Rosario; Warner repeatedly inserts critical or sarcastic parenthetical comments.

subfiles.title: Department of State routing and filing sheet
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Administrative cover or routing sheet associated with a Japanese-press translation report.
subfiles.summary: State Department routing and filing sheet with headings, initials and an April 1, 1944 stamp; no press summary.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, February 17–23, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Military and Naval Attachés in Buenos Aires; U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Report on the Japanese community in Argentina after the rupture of relations, including arrests, business changes, Swiss protection of Japanese interests, and community notices.
subfiles.summary: Translations, February 17-23, 1944: Japanese reaction to espionage allegations and the release of Rosario detainees, horticultural association leadership changes, closing businesses and the Japan Tourist Bureau, the Swiss Legation's new section for Japanese interests, and Bolivian confiscation threats.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, March 1–6, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Military and Naval Attachés in Buenos Aires; U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Report on Japanese Association business, community schools and clubs, espionage suspects, personal notices, and donations.
subfiles.summary: Translations, March 1-6, 1944: the Japanese Association's annual meeting, Cosquin Sanatorium budget, dropped land purchases and possible repatriation; closures, school and youth-club notices; Japanese held as espionage suspects and a baseball donors' list read as alluding to prisoners.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, March 14–20, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State and other U.S. officials
subfiles.about: Detailed report on the Japanese Association’s annual business and finances, followed by community notices and warnings about a confidence man.
subfiles.summary: The Association’s officers describe their activities during the year in which Argentina broke relations with Japan, including memorial services, earthquake relief, library growth, and membership statistics. Treasurer Sadao Hattori supplies a lengthy balance sheet covering the Association building, Cosquín Sanatorium, the Burzaco recreation ground, equipment, bank accounts, funds, and a year-end deficit. Later translations warn that confidence men—particularly a person using the names Akio Kawase, Shigeyoshi Bise, and Henri Bustamante—were exploiting the closure of the Japanese consulate.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, March 21–27, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State; Office of Strategic Services and other U.S. officials
subfiles.about: Report on Japanese Association elections and varied community, business, travel, and political notices.
subfiles.summary: Translations, March 21-27, 1944: voting at the Japanese Association's nineteenth meeting, replacement of commercial representatives if an exchange ship prompted repatriation, Heizo Taira's inquiry into nephew Shigeru Bise, a burned Misiones home, Argentine military-police recruitment publicity, and Cordoba association officers.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, February 11–16, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Military and Naval Attachés in Buenos Aires; U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Report on Japanese reactions to arrests and espionage investigations following Argentina’s break with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Translations, February 11-16, 1944: papers deny rumors, urge calm and advise avoiding police attention; Argentina struggled to translate Japanese and coded communications, with seven civilians and two naval officers arrested; Sweden's representation of Argentine interests, Rosario arrests, repatriation seekers and gifted embassy furniture.

subfiles.title: Letter on routing Japanese-press reports
subfiles.to: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Instructions to redirect future Japanese-press reports because their former State Department recipients had left or changed assignments.
subfiles.summary: Hanley notes Selden Chapin went to Algiers and John Toop resigned to join the Navy, and asks Warner to address future copies to the Foreign Activity Correlation chief or the Office of American Republic Affairs director.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese press in Argentina
subfiles.about: Brief memorandum identifying two significant themes in attached embassy summaries of the Japanese press in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Argentina accepted funds Japanese residents collected after relations broke, and Japanese papers stayed free to praise the Farrell government and criticize American countries that hadn't recognized it.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, April 11–17, 1944
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, Second Secretary, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.to: Military and Naval Attachés in Buenos Aires; U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Report on Japanese community clubs, churches, business associations, donations, leadership changes, and pro-Argentine editorials.
subfiles.summary: The report lists new Japanese Youth’s Club officers, travel and business notices, a death, tennis teams, and statistics for the Japanese Christian Church. The Laundry and Cleaners Trade Association suspends operations after Argentina’s rupture with Japan, while Sadao Hattori hosts an inaugural gathering as the Japanese Association’s new president. Other prominent items concern former consul Chihiro Uchida’s gifts, the Argentine Army’s acceptance of a Japanese-funded air-raid-defense contribution, the escape of Graf Spee sailors, and editorials praising the Farrell government and Argentine neutrality.

subfiles.title: Translations from the Japanese press, June 16–30, 1944, opening page
subfiles.to: Military, Naval, and Legal Attachés in Buenos Aires; U.S. Embassy Santiago; U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Opening page of a report on local Japanese-press items from the second half of June 1944.
subfiles.summary: Translations, June 16-30, 1944, first page: an editorial attacks one-sided Argentine reporting of the European invasion, the Buenos Aires Japanese school's charity gift for La Rioja and Catamarca, Republican House gains, and the start of an editorial on an alleged attack on California internees.
